content_voiceover: This slide illustrates PNH mosaicism, which is a high yield concept. Patients don't have a single uniform population of abnormal cells, instead they have a mosaic of type one cells which are normal, type two cells with partial PIGA deficiency and partial loss of GPI anchored proteins, and type three cells with complete PIGA deficiency and complete loss. The proportion of type three cells drives the clinical picture, a patient dominated by type three cells has high grade intravascular hemolysis, while a patient with mostly type one and only a small type three population has minimal hemolysis. This mosaicism is also dynamic and can shift over time. The table on the right, from a study of eighty PNH patients, shows how varied the presentation can be, symptoms of anemia in about a third, hemoglobinuria in about a quarter, and thrombosis or embolism in only six percent, even though thrombosis is the most feared and lethal complication. Aplastic anemia features in thirteen percent, reflecting the close relationship between PNH and bone marrow failure syndromes. The takeaway for boards, don't expect classic hemoglobinuria in every PNH patient, presentation is heterogeneous and clone size correlates with hemolytic severity.
keypoints: Type I = normal, II = partial PIGA deficiency, III = complete PIGA deficiency
% type III clone correlates with hemolysis severity
PNH clone size is dynamic, changes over time
Only ~26% present with hemoglobinuria; only 6% with thrombosis
13% present as aplastic anemia — PNH/AA overlap
keypoint_voiceover: Key testable point, PNH cells come in three flow cytometry types, type one is normal, type two has partial PIGA gene deficiency, and type three has complete deficiency with no GPI anchored proteins at all. The percentage of type three cells determines how severe the hemolysis is. Clinical presentation is heterogeneous, only about a quarter of patients present with classic hemoglobinuria, while thirteen percent present as aplastic anemia, highlighting the tight link between PNH and bone marrow failure. Clone size can also change dynamically over time, so a single measurement doesn't capture the full picture.
